claim: The human gut microbiome plays a prominent role in xenobiotic transformation.
source: Although the human gut microbiome plays a prominent role in xenobiotic transformation, most of the genes and enzymes responsible for this metabolism are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract introduction

claim: Most of the genes and enzymes responsible for xenobiotic metabolism by the gut microbiome are unknown.
source: Although the human gut microbiome plays a prominent role in xenobiotic transformation, most of the genes and enzymes responsible for this metabolism are unknown.
evidence: This is stated as a knowledge gap in the abstract

claim: The two-gene 'cardiac glycoside reductase' (cgr) operon encoded by Eggerthella lenta is linked to inactivation of digoxin.
source: Recently, we linked the two-gene 'cardiac glycoside reductase' ( cgr ) operon encoded by the gut Actinobacterium Eggerthella lenta to inactivation of the cardiac medication and plant natural product digoxin.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding by the authors, supported by citation to previous work

claim: An expanded 8-gene cgr-associated gene cluster is present in all digoxin metabolizers and absent in non-metabolizers among 25 E. lenta strains and close relatives.
source: Here, we compared the genomes of 25 E. lenta strains and close relatives, revealing an expanded 8-gene cgr -associated gene cluster present in all digoxin metabolizers and absent in non-metabolizers.
evidence: This is supported by comparative genomics data presented in the manuscript, including Figure 1C-D

claim: A single flavin- and [4Fe-4S] cluster-dependent reductase, Cgr2, is sufficient for digoxin inactivation.
source: Using heterologous expression and in vitro biochemical characterization, we discovered that a single flavin- and [4Fe-4S] cluster-dependent reductase, Cgr2, is sufficient for digoxin inactivation.
evidence: This is supported by heterologous expression experiments (Figure 2A) and in vitro biochemical assays throughout the manuscript

claim: Cgr2 displayed strict specificity for digoxin and other cardenolides.
source: Unexpectedly, Cgr2 displayed strict specificity for digoxin and other cardenolides.
evidence: This is supported by substrate specificity assays shown in Figure 4

claim: The cgr2 gene is widespread and conserved in the human population.
source: Quantification of cgr2 in gut microbiomes revealed that this gene is widespread and conserved in the human population.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis of 1872 individuals and qPCR validation shown in Figure 6

claim: Human-associated gut bacteria maintain specialized enzymes that protect against ingested plant toxins.
source: Together, these results demonstrate that human-associated gut bacteria maintain specialized enzymes that protect against ingested plant toxins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strict specificity of Cgr2 for cardenolides (plant toxins) and its widespread distribution

claim: Human gut bacteria reduce digoxin to the inactive metabolite dihydrodigoxin, decreasing drug efficacy and toxicity.
source: It has been known for decades that human gut bacteria reduce digoxin to the inactive metabolite dihydrodigoxin, decreasing drug efficacy and toxicity
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Saha et al., 1983; Lindenbaum et al., 1981a; Lindenbaum et al., 1981b)

claim: Only two isolates capable of metabolizing digoxin were found from screening hundreds of gut bacterial strains, both of which were strains of Eggerthella lenta.
source: Screening hundreds of gut bacterial strains from humans that excreted high levels of dihydrodigoxin revealed only two isolates that were capable of metabolizing digoxin, both of which were strains of the anaerobic, low abundance bacterium Eggerthella lenta
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Saha et al., 1983)

claim: The presence of E. lenta in the gut microbiome cannot accurately predict digoxin reduction activity, as patients colonized by E. lenta show marked variation in dihydrodigoxin production.
source: However, the presence of E. lenta in the gut microbiome cannot accurately predict this reactivity, as patients colonized by E. lenta still show marked variation in dihydrodigoxin production
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior clinical observations (Mathan et al., 1989; Alam et al., 1988)

claim: Strain-level variations in the E. lenta population and inhibition of bacterial drug metabolism by dietary amino acids are two mechanisms underlying variation in dihydrodigoxin production.
source: We identified two mechanisms underlying this discrepancy: strain-level variations in the E. lenta population and inhibition of bacterial drug metabolism by dietary amino acids.
evidence: This is stated as a prior finding by the authors

claim: Digoxin induces expression of a 2-gene operon in E. lenta DSM 2243, named the cardiac glycoside reductase (cgr) operon.
source: Digoxin induces expression of a 2-gene operon encoded by the type strain of E. lenta (DSM 2243), which we named the cardiac glycoside reductase (cgr) operon
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013)

claim: The cgr operon was absent in two E. lenta strains that did not metabolize digoxin.
source: The cgr operon was absent in two E. lenta strains that did not metabolize digoxin ('non-reducing' strains)
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013)

claim: cgr operon presence and abundance predicted the extent of drug inactivation by human gut microbial communities in ex vivo incubations.
source: cgr operon presence and abundance predicted the extent of drug inactivation by human gut microbial communities in ex vivo incubations
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013)

claim: Germ-free mice mono-colonized by a reducing (cgr+) strain of E. lenta had lower serum levels of digoxin than mice colonized by a non-reducing (cgr-) strain.
source: Furthermore, germ-free mice that had been mono-colonized by a reducing (cgr+) strain of E. lenta had lower serum levels of digoxin than mice colonized by a non-reducing (cgr-) strain
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013; Haiser et al., 2014)

claim: Dietary arginine efficiently blocked digoxin reduction by the cgr operon in cgr+ E. lenta-colonized mice.
source: dietary arginine efficiently blocked digoxin reduction by the cgr operon in cgr+ E. lenta-colonized mice
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013; Haiser et al., 2014)

claim: The collection of 25 E. lenta and closely related Coriobacteriia strains were isolated from 22 individuals in 6 countries across three continents spanning the years of 1938–2015.
source: These bacteria were isolated from 22 individuals in 6 countries across three continents spanning the years of 1938–2015 (Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by strain collection metadata in Figure 1—source data 1

claim: Seven additional strains capable of digoxin inactivation were identified beyond the original E. lenta DSM 2243 strain.
source: We used liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS) to quantify the biotransformation of digoxin to dihydrodigoxin by each strain and identified seven additional strains capable of drug inactivation (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by LC-MS/MS data shown in Figure 1A

claim: Culturing experiments were performed using 10 µM of digoxin, which is within the estimated range (0.4–14.6 µM) of therapeutic concentrations of the drug in the gut prior to absorption by host epithelial cells.
source: Culturing experiments were performed using 10 µM of digoxin, which is within the estimated range (0.4–14.6 µM) of therapeutic concentrations of the drug in the gut prior to absorption by host epithelial cells
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work (Schiller et al., 2005)

claim: The digoxin metabolizing strains did not exhibit a significant phylogenetic signal (p=0.275, K = 0.049, Blomberg's K test).
source: The digoxin metabolizing strains did not exhibit a significant phylogenetic signal (Figure 1B; p=0.275, K = 0.049, Blomberg's K test)
evidence: This is supported by phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 1B with statistical test results

claim: The phenotypic trait of digoxin metabolism has been gained (or lost) multiple times over the course of E. lenta evolution.
source: suggesting that this phenotypic trait has been gained (or lost) multiple times over the course of E. lenta evolution.
evidence: This is inferred from the lack of phylogenetic signal in digoxin metabolism

claim: Machine learning (random forests) analysis of orthologous gene cluster presence/absence revealed a single genetic locus with 100% discriminative value between metabolizers and non-metabolizers.
source: Machine learning (random forests) analysis of orthologous gene cluster presence/absence across the strain collection revealed a single genetic locus with 100% discriminative value between metabolizers and non-metabolizers (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by random forest analysis shown in Figure 1C

claim: The cgr gene cluster includes the previously identified 2-gene cgr operon (cgr1 and cgr2) and six neighboring genes termed cac (cgr-associated cluster) genes.
source: This locus, referred to hereafter as the cgr gene cluster, includes the previously identified 2-gene cgr operon (cgr1 and cgr2) and six neighboring genes termed cac (cgr-associated cluster) genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by genomic context analysis shown in Figure 1D

claim: The cac genes include a putative LuxR type transcriptional regulator (Cac3), a predicted flavin-dependent fumarate reductase (Cac4), three proteins of unknown function (Cac1, Cac5, Cac6), and a short protein (Cac2) that is conserved in both cgr- and cgr+ strains of E. lenta.
source: The cac genes include a putative LuxR type transcriptional regulator (Cac3), a predicted flavin-dependent fumarate reductase (Cac4), three proteins of unknown function (Cac1, Cac5, Cac6), and a short protein (Cac2) that is conserved in both cgr- and cgr+ strains of E. lenta.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic annotation of the gene cluster

claim: The 10.4 kb cgr gene cluster was highly conserved between strains with an average global nucleotide identity of 99.95 ± 0.05% (mean ± standard deviation).
source: The 10.4 kb cgr gene cluster was highly conserved between strains with an average global nucleotide identity of 99.95 ± 0.05% (mean ± standard deviation (SD)).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison data

claim: Only the cgr operon (cgr1 and cgr2) is highly upregulated (>165 fold) in response to digoxin, whereas cac4 is not significantly induced (1.3-fold change relative to vehicle controls, p=0.83).
source: RNA sequencing (Haiser et al., 2013) demonstrated that the cgr operon (cgr1 and cgr2) is highly upregulated (>165 fold) in response to digoxin, whereas cac4 is not significantly induced (1.3-fold change relative to vehicle controls, p=0.83) (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1E

claim: The remainder of the cgr-associated cluster is largely transcriptionally dormant during exponential growth both with and without the presence of digoxin (<6 normalized counts per gene).
source: The remainder of the cgr-associated cluster is largely transcriptionally dormant during exponential growth both with and without the presence of digoxin (<6 normalized counts per gene) and is therefore unlikely to be linked to digoxin metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data

claim: Cgr1 is a putative membrane-anchored protein that belongs to the cytochrome c3 superfamily (Pfam 14537) and is predicted to harbor covalently bound heme groups (CXXCH motif).
source: Cgr1 is a putative membrane-anchored protein that belongs to the cytochrome c3 superfamily (Pfam 14537) and is predicted to harbor covalently bound heme groups (CXXCH motif).
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic sequence analysis

claim: Cgr1 most closely resembles the NapC/NirT (NrfH) family of proteins that transfer electrons from the membrane quinone pool to associated reductases.
source: It most closely resembles the NapC/NirT (NrfH) family of proteins that transfer electrons from the membrane quinone pool to associated reductases, facilitating reduction of terminal electron acceptors such as nitrite and sulfite
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity and supported by citations (Kemp et al., 2010; Kern et al., 2008)

claim: A close homolog of Cgr1 (Elen_2528) exists in E. lenta DSM 2243 (91.75% amino acid identity, BLASTP) that is a component of the E. lenta core genome (99.39 ± 0.81% global identity mean ± SD).
source: We also identified a close homolog of Cgr1 (Elen_2528) in E. lenta DSM 2243 (91.75% amino acid identity, BLASTP) that is a component of the E. lenta core genome (99.39 ± 0.81% global identity mean ± SD).
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison data

claim: The presence of a highly similar protein to Cgr1 in both metabolizing and non-metabolizing strains indicates that Cgr1 is involved in a more general function (e.g. electron transfer, membrane docking) rather than direct reduction of digoxin.
source: The presence of this highly similar protein in both metabolizing and non-metabolizing strains further indicates that Cgr1 is involved in a more general function (e.g. electron transfer, membrane docking) rather than direct reduction of digoxin.
evidence: This is inferred from the presence of a Cgr1 homolog in non-metabolizing strains

claim: Cgr2 is unique to the genomes of cgr+ E. lenta, and the closest homologs of Cgr2 display <28% amino acid identity.
source: On the other hand, Cgr2 is unique to the genomes of cgr+ E. lenta, and the closest homologs of Cgr2 display <28% amino acid identity.
evidence: This is supported by sequence comparison data

claim: Cgr2 is a homolog of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent fumarate reductases (Pfam 00890; Interpro 003953/027477).
source: Cgr2 is a homolog of flavin adenine dinucleotide (FAD)-dependent fumarate reductases (Pfam 00890; Interpro 003953/027477)
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic annotation

claim: Cgr2 is predicted to undergo secretion via the twin arginine translocation (Tat) pathway.
source: and is predicted to undergo secretion via the twin arginine translocation (Tat) pathway.
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic prediction

claim: Cgr1 and Cgr2 form a membrane-associated complex that catalyzes reduction of the α,β-unsaturated butyrolactone of digoxin.
source: Taken together, these observations led us to hypothesize that Cgr1 and Cgr2 form a membrane-associated complex that catalyzes reduction of the α,β-unsaturated butyrolactone of digoxin.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on bioinformatic analysis and prior knowledge

claim: Cgr2 expressing strains showed a significant increase in dihydrodigoxin levels relative to empty vector controls in R. erythropolis.
source: The Cgr2 expressing strains showed a significant increase in dihydrodigoxin levels relative to empty vector controls (Figure 2A; Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by heterologous expression data shown in Figure 2A

claim: No activity was observed for the strain expressing only Cgr1 in R. erythropolis.
source: In contrast, no activity was observed for the strain expressing only Cgr1
evidence: This is supported by heterologous expression data

claim: Cgr2 is sufficient for digoxin reduction in R. erythropolis cells.
source: These results show that Cgr2 is sufficient for digoxin reduction in R. erythropolis cells
evidence: This is concluded from heterologous expression experiments

claim: Endogenous redox active proteins and/or metabolites in R. erythropolis may fulfill the putative function of Cgr1 as an electron donor.
source: and endogenous redox active proteins and/or metabolites in this heterologous host may fulfill the putative function of Cgr1 as an electron donor.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Cgr2 alone is sufficient for activity in the heterologous host

claim: The three motifs required for flavin cofactor binding are conserved in all 8 Cgr2 sequences.
source: Computational analysis of Cgr2 predicted that it would bind flavin through a Rossmann fold (Dym and Eisenberg, 2001), and the three motifs required for cofactor binding are conserved in all 8 Cgr2 sequences (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by computational analysis and sequence alignment shown in Figure 2B

claim: Cgr2 did not co-purify with flavin.
source: However, Cgr2 did not co-purify with flavin.
evidence: This is an observation from protein purification experiments

claim: Cgr2 obtained from initial purifications was thermally unstable (melting temperature <37°C).
source: Moreover, Cgr2 obtained from initial purifications was thermally unstable (melting temperature <37°C)
evidence: This is supported by thermal denaturation assay data

claim: Purified Cgr2 was light brown in color, suggesting the presence of a metallocofactor.
source: We also noticed that purified Cgr2 was light brown in color, suggesting the presence of a metallocofactor.
evidence: This is an observation that leads to inference about metallocofactor presence

claim: Cgr2 contains 16 cysteines in the mature sequence.
source: The combination of the brown color and the presence of 16 cysteines in the mature Cgr2 sequence led us to hypothesize that this enzyme contained one or more [Fe-S] clusters.
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis

claim: No canonical [2Fe-2S], [3Fe-4Fe], or [4Fe-4S] cluster binding motifs were detected within the Cgr2 sequence.
source: However, we were unable to detect any canonical [2Fe-2S], [3Fe-4Fe], or [4Fe-4S] cluster binding motifs within the Cgr2 sequence (Figure 2—source data 3)
evidence: This is based on bioinformatic motif analysis

claim: Chemical reconstitution of [Fe-S] cluster formation by incubating Cgr2 with iron and sulfide under anaerobic conditions greatly improved protein stability.
source: Attempts to chemically reconstitute [Fe-S] cluster formation by incubating Cgr2 with iron and sulfide under anaerobic conditions greatly improved protein stability (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–D

claim: Including FAD in assay mixtures dramatically increased the digoxin reduction activity of purified protein.
source: In addition to performing this reconstitution step, including FAD in assay mixtures dramatically increased the digoxin reduction activity of purified protein (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 2C

claim: Even after reconstitution, Cgr2 required excess FAD for maximal activity.
source: Even after reconstitution, Cgr2 required excess FAD for maximal activity
evidence: This is an observation from activity assays

claim: Cgr1 could be important for enhancing FAD binding, as has been observed for proteins whose FAD-binding site is predicted to occur at the interface of two domains.
source: suggesting that Cgr1 could be important for enhancing FAD binding, as has been observed for proteins whose FAD-binding site is predicted to occur at the interface of two domains
evidence: This is speculation based on analogy to other proteins, supported by citation (Kleven et al., 2015)

claim: Prior to reconstitution, purified Cgr2 contained between 0.2–0.6 equivalents of iron and sulfide.
source: Prior to reconstitution, purified Cgr2 contained between 0.2–0.6 equivalents of iron and sulfide
evidence: This is supported by colorimetric assay data

claim: The UV-vis spectrum of unreconstituted Cgr2 displayed absorption features consistent with the presence of low levels of [Fe-S] clusters.
source: and its ultraviolet-visible (UV-vis) spectrum displayed absorption features consistent with the presence of low levels of [Fe-S] clusters (Ayala-Castro et al., 2008) (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by UV-vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D

claim: After reconstitution, Cgr2 exhibited a broad peak around 400 nm that decreased in absorbance upon addition of sodium dithionite.
source: After reconstitution, Cgr2 exhibited a broad peak around 400 nm (Figure 2D) that decreased in absorbance upon addition of an excess amount of the reducing agent sodium dithionite (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This is supported by UV-vis spectroscopy data

claim: The spectral properties of reconstituted Cgr2 are characteristic of redox-active [Fe-S] clusters.
source: These spectral properties are characteristic of redox-active [Fe-S] clusters.
evidence: This is an interpretation of UV-vis spectroscopy data based on established knowledge

claim: Exposure of reconstituted Cgr2 to oxygen led to [Fe-S] cluster decomposition as evidenced by a decrease in the absorbance at 400 nm.
source: Exposure of reconstituted Cgr2 to oxygen led to [Fe-S] cluster decomposition as evidenced by a decrease in the absorbance at 400 nm (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by UV-vis spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2D

claim: The [Fe-S] cluster(s) of Cgr2 are oxygen-sensitive.
source: demonstrating that the [Fe-S] cluster(s) of Cgr2 are oxygen-sensitive.
evidence: This is concluded from oxygen exposure experiments

claim: In the absence of a reducing agent, purified, unreconstituted Cgr2 does not have an EPR signal.
source: In the absence of a reducing agent, purified, unreconstituted Cgr2 does not have an EPR signal (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy data

claim: Upon reduction with sodium dithionite, the EPR spectrum of Cgr2 exhibits a signal with axial symmetry and with principal g-components of 2.045 and 1.94.
source: Upon reduction with sodium dithionite, the EPR spectrum of Cgr2 exhibits a signal with axial symmetry and with principal g-components of 2.045 and 1.94.
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy data

claim: The EPR signal increases in intensity upon reconstitution of Cgr2 (10 K), and is barely detectable above 40 K.
source: This signal increases in intensity upon reconstitution of Cgr2 (10 K), and is barely detectable above 40 K (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by EPR spectroscopy data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The principal g-values and the relaxation properties (temperature dependence) of the EPR signal are characteristic of low-potential tetranuclear [4Fe-4S]1+ centers.
source: Both the principal g-values and the relaxation properties (temperature dependence) of this signal are characteristic of low-potential tetranuclear [4Fe-4S]1+ centers.
evidence: This is an interpretation of EPR data based on established knowledge

claim: Cgr2 contains [4Fe-4S]2+ cluster that can undergo reduction to the corresponding [4Fe-4S]1+ state.
source: These observations indicate that Cgr2 contains [4Fe-4S]2+ cluster that can undergo reduction to the corresponding [4Fe-4S]1+ state.
evidence: This is concluded from EPR spectroscopy data

claim: The redox properties of the [4Fe-4S] cluster(s) suggest that they may participate in catalysis (electron transfer).
source: These redox properties suggest that these [4Fe-4S] cluster(s) may participate in catalysis (electron transfer).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed redox properties

claim: Purified, unreconstituted Cgr2 contains 0.02–0.03 [4Fe-4S]1+ clusters per protein monomer.
source: Using a Cu2+-EDTA standard, we determined that purified, unreconstituted Cgr2 contains 0.02–0.03 [4Fe-4S]1+ clusters per protein monomer.
evidence: This is supported by EPR quantification data

claim: After reconstitution with iron and sulfide, the intensity of the EPR signal increased to 0.13–0.25 [4Fe-4S]1+ clusters per Cgr2.
source: After reconstitution with iron and sulfide, the intensity of the EPR signal increased to 0.13–0.25 [4Fe-4S]1+ clusters per Cgr2.
evidence: This is supported by EPR quantification data

claim: The in vitro activity of Cgr2 increases upon reconstitution with increasing equivalents of iron and sulfide.
source: Indeed, the in vitro activity of Cgr2 increases upon reconstitution with increasing equivalents of iron and sulfide (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data

claim: Six cysteine residues, when mutated to alanine, significantly decreased dihydrodigoxin production by both heterologously expressed and purified Cgr2.
source: Individually mutating each of the 16 cysteines present in wild-type Cgr2 to alanine revealed six residues that, when mutated, significantly decreased dihydrodigoxin production by both heterologously expressed and purified Cgr2
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: EPR analysis of six Cgr2 cysteine mutants revealed comparable levels of [4Fe-4S]1+ cluster incorporation relative to the wild-type enzyme.
source: EPR analysis of these six Cgr2 mutants revealed comparable levels of [4Fe-4S]1+ cluster incorporation relative to the wild-type enzyme (Figure 2—figure supplement 3D)
evidence: This is supported by EPR data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3D

claim: A range of divalent metal cations (Fe2+, Mn2+, Mg2+) stimulated the activity of Cgr2 in vitro.
source: Consistent with this latter proposal, we found that a range of divalent metal cations (Fe2+, Mn2+, Mg2+) stimulated the activity of Cgr2 in vitro (Figure 2—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3E

claim: Fe2+ stimulated the in vitro activity of only 3 out of 6 impaired cysteine mutants (C158A, C187A, C327A).
source: Additionally, Fe2+ stimulated the in vitro activity of only 3 out of 6 impaired mutants (C158A, C187A, C327A) (Figure 2—figure supplement 3F).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3F

claim: Binding of digoxin to its target in human cells, Na+/K+ ATPase, is thought to be mediated by long-range electrostatic interactions between a Mg2+ ion and the electron rich, partially negatively charged oxygen atom of the unsaturated lactone.
source: Notably, binding of digoxin to its target in human cells, Na+/K+ ATPase, is thought to be mediated by long-range electrostatic interactions between a Mg2+ ion and the electron rich, partially negatively charged oxygen atom of the unsaturated lactone
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work (Laursen et al., 2015; Weigand et al., 2014)

claim: Only two cgr2 nucleotide variants were detected among E. lenta genomes, which were validated by targeted Sanger sequencing.
source: Strikingly, only two cgr2 nucleotide variants were detected, which were validated by targeted Sanger sequencing.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data

claim: One cgr2 variant is only found in the DSM 2243 type strain resulting in a conservative methionine (M) to valine (V) substitution at position 381.
source: One of these variants is only found in the DSM 2243 type strain resulting in a conservative methionine (M) to valine (V) substitution at position 381.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data

claim: The other cgr2 variant results in either aromatic tyrosine (Y) as in the type strain DSM 2243 or neutral asparagine (N) at position 333.
source: The other results in either aromatic tyrosine (Y) as in the type strain DSM 2243 or neutral asparagine (N) at position 333 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis data shown in Figure 3A

claim: 14 additional cgr2 sequences were fully or partially reconstructed from 96 gut microbiome datasets with a high abundance of E. lenta.
source: We were also able to fully or partially reconstruct 14 additional cgr2 sequences using reads mapping to the cgr gene cluster from 96 gut microbiome datasets with a high abundance of E. lenta (>1x coverage or >0.001 proportional abundance).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis

claim: Metagenome fragments confirmed the presence of both Y333 and N333 variants in a 9:5 ratio.
source: These metagenome fragments confirmed the presence of both Y333 and N333 variants in a 9:5 ratio (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 3A

claim: The DSM 2243 M381 variant was not observed in metagenomic analysis.
source: while the DSM 2243 M381 variant was not observed.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis

claim: 49 metagenomes with at least one read mapping over the variant position confirmed the bi-allelic nature with 15 Y333 and 34 N333 metagenomes.
source: This uncovered 49 metagenomes with at least one read mapping over the variant position, confirming the bi-allelic nature with 15 Y333 and 34 N333 metagenomes.
evidence: This is supported by assembly-free variant calling from metagenomic data

claim: Nearly all metagenomes (41/42) with reads mapping to position 381 supported the valine residue suggesting that the DSM 2243 M381 variant is rare.
source: Nearly all metagenomes (41/42) with reads mapping to position 381 supported the valine residue suggesting that the DSM 2243 M381 variant is rare.
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis

claim: cgr2 is at the 67th percentile of conservation in the context of the E. lenta pan-genome (based on 24 sequenced isolates).
source: Given that this analysis confirmed the highly conserved nature of the cgr locus, we analyzed the conservation of cgr2 in the context of the E. lenta pan-genome (based on 24 sequenced isolates) finding that it is at the 67th percentile of conservation.
evidence: This is supported by pan-genome analysis shown in Figure 3C

claim: E. lenta strains encoding the N333 variant show a trend towards a decreased ability to metabolize digoxin as compared to Y333-encoding strains (p=0.052 Welch's t-test).
source: E. lenta strains encoding the N333 variant show a trend towards a decreased ability to metabolize digoxin as compared to Y333-encoding strains (Figure 3D; Figure 3—source data 1; p=0.052 Welch's t-test).
evidence: This is supported by activity assay data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The decreased activity of N333 variant was more readily apparent following incubation of digoxin with Cgr2 proteins in vitro.
source: This decreased activity was more readily apparent following incubation of digoxin with Cgr2 proteins in vitro (Figure 3E; Figure 3—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro activity assay data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Kinetic parameters for wild-type Cgr2 (Y333) were KM = 94.6 ± 7.1 µM and a catalytic efficiency of 2.4 ± 0.8×103 M−1 s−1.
source: While kinetic parameters for wild-type Cgr2 (Y333) were KM = 94.6 ± 7.1 µM and a catalytic efficiency of 2.4 ± 0.8×103 M−1 s−1
evidence: This is supported by kinetic assay data

claim: Saturating Vmax conditions could not be reached for the N333 variant within the range of concentrations where digoxin is soluble (≤0.5 mM).
source: saturating Vmax conditions could not be reached for the N333 variant within the range of concentrations where digoxin is soluble (≤0.5 mM).
evidence: This is an observation from kinetic assays

claim: Despite its lower activity, Cgr2 N333 converted digoxin to dihydrodigoxin at a comparable efficiency to Y333 after 4.5 hr.
source: Despite its lower activity, Cgr2 N333 converted digoxin to dihydrodigoxin at a comparable efficiency to Y333 after 4.5 hr (Figure 3F; Figure 3—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by endpoint activity assay data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Compared to the activity of other FAD-dependent reductases towards their native substrates, the Y333 Cgr2 variant is less efficient for digoxin reduction.
source: Compared to the activity of other FAD-dependent reductases towards their native substrates, the Y333 Cgr2 variant is less efficient for digoxin reduction
evidence: This is based on comparison with literature values for other reductases

claim: Cgr2 displayed robust activity only toward cardenolides, the family of plant toxins that includes the pharmaceutical agents digoxin and digitoxin as well as ouabain.
source: Cgr2 displayed robust activity only toward cardenolides, the family of plant toxins that includes the pharmaceutical agents digoxin and digitoxin as well as ouabain, which is used as an arrowhead poison
evidence: This is supported by substrate specificity assays shown in Figure 4

claim: The cardenolide aglycones digoxigenin and ouabagenin were metabolized at a significantly faster rate than their glycosylated forms digoxin and ouabain, respectively (p<0.01, Student's t test).
source: The cardenolide aglycones digoxigenin and ouabagenin were metabolized at a significantly faster rate than their glycosylated forms digoxin and ouabain, respectively (**p<0.01, Student's t test).
evidence: This is supported by substrate specificity assay data

claim: The isolated lactone 2(5H)-furanone was minimally processed by Cgr2, indicating that an intact steroid core is important for activity.
source: The isolated lactone 2(5H)-furanone was minimally processed by Cgr2, indicating that an intact steroid core is important for activity.
evidence: This is concluded from substrate specificity assays

claim: The qualitatively similar rates observed for reduction of the various cardenolides demonstrates that the enzyme tolerates differences in the number and position of hydroxyl groups on the steroid scaffold.
source: However, the qualitatively similar rates observed for reduction of the various cardenolides demonstrates that the enzyme tolerates differences in the number and position of hydroxyl groups on the steroid scaffold.
evidence: This is concluded from substrate specificity assays

claim: Cgr2 activity is restricted to cardenolide toxins and does not extend to other structurally related endogenous or exogenous compounds.
source: Overall, these results suggest that Cgr2 activity is restricted to cardenolide toxins and does not extend to other structurally related endogenous or exogenous compounds.
evidence: This is concluded from substrate specificity assays shown in Figure 4

claim: Neither fumarate nor any of the metabolized cardenolides conferred a growth advantage to cgr2+ E. lenta in minimal or rich medias.
source: Additionally, neither fumarate nor any of the metabolized cardenolides conferred a growth advantage to cgr2+ E. lenta in minimal or rich medias, suggesting that these compounds are not used as alternative terminal electron acceptors (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by growth assay data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: The inability of Cgr2 to reduce fumarate led to revisiting the original annotation of Cgr2 as a 'fumarate reductase'.
source: The inability of Cgr2 to reduce fumarate, a common electron acceptor used during bacterial anaerobic respiration, led us to revisit the original annotation of Cgr2 as a 'fumarate reductase'
evidence: This is based on the observation that Cgr2 does not reduce fumarate

claim: Within the sequence similarity network, there were seven enzymes that had been biochemically characterized, biochemically and structurally characterized, or genetically characterized.
source: Within the network, there were seven enzymes that had been biochemically characterized (UniProtKB IDs: Q07WU7, Q9Z4P0, 8CVD0, P71864), biochemically and structurally characterized (PDB IDs: 1D4D, 1E39), or genetically characterized (UniProtKB ID: Q7D5C1)
evidence: This is based on sequence similarity network analysis

claim: At all thresholds at which Cgr2 remained connected to other protein sequences, all characterized enzymes within the SSN were co-clustered, precluding the resolution of unique biochemical functions at this cutoff.
source: At all thresholds at which Cgr2 remained connected to other protein sequences, all characterized enzymes within the SSN were co-clustered, precluding the resolution of unique biochemical functions at this cutoff (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence similarity network analysis shown in Figure 5A

claim: At higher alignment thresholds that separated characterized enzymes into discrete isofunctional clusters, Cgr2 was always present as a 'singleton' with no links to other protein sequences.
source: At higher alignment thresholds that separated these characterized enzymes into discrete isofunctional clusters, Cgr2 was always present as a 'singleton' with no links to other protein sequences (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by sequence similarity network analysis shown in Figure 5B

claim: Reductase enzymes are widespread among human gut bacteria, with three validated enzymatic activities and 113 distinct clusters with uncharacterized biochemical functions detected in sequenced gut bacterial genomes.
source: Our SSN also revealed that reductase enzymes are widespread among human gut bacteria, with three validated enzymatic activities and 113 distinct clusters with uncharacterized biochemical functions detected in sequenced gut bacterial genomes.
evidence: This is supported by sequence similarity network analysis

claim: Cgr2 lacks active site residues required for the activity of fumarate reductases (6/7 divergent residues), urocanate reductases (4/5 divergent residues), and ketosteroid dehydrogenases (3/5 divergent residues).
source: Comparing the sequence of Cgr2 with sequences of biochemically characterized reductases revealed that Cgr2 lacks active site residues required for the activity of fumarate reductases (6/7 divergent residues), urocanate reductases (4/5 divergent residues), and ketosteroid dehydrogenases (3/5 divergent residues)
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4

claim: Individually mutating two residues shared between Cgr2 and ketosteroid dehydrogenases confirmed that one amino acid involved in substrate binding (G536 backbone) was important for the activity of Cgr2 but the other (Y532) was not.
source: Individually mutating the two residues shared between Cgr2 and ketosteroid dehydrogenases confirmed that one amino acid involved in substrate binding (G536 backbone) was also important for the activity of Cgr2 but the other (Y532) was not (Figure 5—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: This is supported by site-directed mutagenesis data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4E

claim: The location of Cgr2 within the SSN and the differences in its sequence indicate that this enzyme is distinct from characterized bacterial reductases and may use a unique set of residues to catalyze cardenolide reduction.
source: Together, the location of Cgr2 within the SSN and the differences in its sequence indicate that this enzyme is distinct from characterized bacterial reductases and may use a unique set of residues to catalyze cardenolide reduction.
evidence: This is inferred from sequence similarity network and sequence alignment analyses

claim: E. lenta was detected in 41.5% of subjects at abundances of −3.5 ± 0.58 mean ± SD log10(elnmrk1 copies/cell) in gut microbiome datasets from 1872 individuals.
source: Using this marker gene, we detected E. lenta in 41.5% of subjects at abundances of −3.5 ± 0.58 mean ± SD log10(elnmrk1 copies/cell) (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: Cgr2 was detectable in 48.5% of the E. lenta-positive individuals, while detection occurred in 27.7% of all subjects (−3.7 ± 0.64 mean ± SD log10(cgr2 copies/cell)).
source: Cgr2 was detectable in 48.5% of the E. lenta-positive individuals, while detection occurred in 27.7% of all subjects (−3.7 ± 0.64 mean ± SD log10(cgr2 copies/cell)) (Figure 6A)
evidence: This is supported by metagenomic analysis shown in Figure 6A

claim: The abundance of E. lenta and cgr2 was significantly associated (rho = 0.455, p<0.001).
source: and the abundance of E. lenta and cgr2 was significantly associated (rho = 0.455, p<0.001; Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6B

claim: The distributions were skewed towards participants with less cgr2 than expected based on the abundance of E. lenta (skew = −0.773, p=2.5e-8, n = 375, D'Agostino skewness test).
source: The distributions were skewed towards participants with less cgr2 than expected based on the abundance of E. lenta [(skew = −0.773, p=2.5e-8, n = 375, D'Agostino skewness test of log10(cgr/elnmrk1) with quantifiable elnmrk1 and cgr2]
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of metagenomic data

claim: The skew towards higher E. lenta abundances versus cgr2 is consistent with prior data suggesting that many individuals are colonized by a mixture of cgr2+ and cgr2- E. lenta strains.
source: consistent with prior data suggesting that many individuals are colonized by a mixture of cgr2+ and cgr2- E. lenta strains
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed skew and supported by citation to prior work (Haiser et al., 2013)

claim: Using qPCR, E. lenta was detected in 81.6% of individuals (1.5e7 ± 3.5e6 copies/g feces) and cgr2 in 74.7% (1.5e6 ± 3.5e6 copies/g feces) in an independent set of 158 individuals.
source: Using this more sensitive detection method, we detected E. lenta in 81.6% of individuals (1.5e7 ± 3.5e6 copies/g feces) and cgr2 in 74.7% (1.5e6 ± 3.5e6 copies/g feces) (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C–D

claim: Both the qPCR- and metagenomic sequencing-based analyses show that E. lenta and cgr2 are widely distributed in the human microbiome.
source: Overall, both the qPCR- and metagenomic sequencing-based analyses show that E. lenta and cgr2 are widely distributed in the human microbiome.
evidence: This is concluded from both metagenomic and qPCR analyses

claim: Cgr2 represents a novel flavoprotein reductase, and contains oxygen-sensitive [4Fe-4S] cluster(s) and a divergent set of predicted active site residues.
source: Cgr2 represents a novel flavoprotein reductase, and contains oxygen-sensitive [4Fe-4S] cluster(s) and a divergent set of predicted active site residues.
evidence: This is concluded from biochemical characterization and sequence analysis

claim: The working model is that Cgr1 and Cgr2 form a membrane-anchored, extracellular complex that mediates electron transfer from an electron donor through multiple cytochromes c in Cgr1 to Cgr2, which ultimately reduces the α,β-unsaturated γ-butyrolactone of digoxin and other cardenolides.
source: Our working model is that Cgr1 and Cgr2 form a membrane-anchored, extracellular complex that mediates electron transfer from an electron donor (e.g. the membrane quinone pool) through multiple cytochromes c in Cgr1 to Cgr2, which ultimately reduces the α,β-unsaturated γ-butyrolactone of digoxin and other cardenolides (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a proposed model based on biochemical and bioinformatic data, shown in Figure 7A

claim: The [4Fe-4S]2+ cluster(s) of Cgr2 sequentially transfer electrons to the FAD cofactor, and the resulting hydride equivalent is then transferred to the cardenolide.
source: We propose that the [4Fe-4S]2+ cluster(s) of Cgr2 sequentially transfer electrons to the FAD cofactor. The resulting hydride equivalent is then transferred to the cardenolide, and proton transfer generates the fully reduced γ-butyrolactone (Figure 7B)
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism shown in Figure 7B

claim: The cgr operon and cgr gene cluster are highly conserved, with two naturally occurring variants (frequent: Y333/N333; infrequent: V381/M381).
source: We have demonstrated that E. lenta strains harboring the cgr operon are widespread in the human gut microbiome, which supports the high incidence of dihydrodigoxin production observed clinically. Strikingly, cgr2 and its associated genes are highly conserved, with two naturally occurring variants (frequent: Y333/N333; infrequent: V381/M381).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis of isolates and metagenomes

claim: The conservation of cgr2 is surprising given the strict specificity of Cgr2 towards cardenolides, which are ingested at very low concentrations to minimize toxicity in the context of cardiac therapy.
source: This conservation is surprising given the strict specificity of Cgr2 towards cardenolides, which are ingested at very low concentrations to minimize toxicity in the context of cardiac therapy
evidence: This is an observation that leads to speculation about the evolutionary significance, supported by citations (Smith et al., 1969; Gheorghiade et al., 2004)

claim: Much of the phenotypic variation within E. lenta may be driven by gene gain/loss rather than by genetic polymorphisms.
source: These results, together with the overall high degree of conservation in the E. lenta pan-genome, suggest that much of the phenotypic variation within this species may be driven by gene gain/loss rather than by genetic polymorphisms.
evidence: This is inferred from the high sequence conservation and pan-genome analysis

claim: The high sequence conservation and levels of cgr operon transcription in response to digoxin exposure suggest that digoxin metabolism may provide a physiological benefit to E. lenta.
source: The high sequence conservation and levels of cgr operon transcription in response to digoxin exposure suggest that digoxin metabolism may provide a physiological benefit to E. lenta.
evidence: This is speculation based on observed conservation and transcriptional response

claim: E. lenta may have evolved to protect the host from plant toxins and thus maintain a habitat for colonization.
source: However, as we could not observe any direct benefit of cardenolide metabolism for cgr+ E. lenta (Figure 4—figure supplement 2), we hypothesize that these bacteria may have evolved to protect the host from plant toxins and thus maintain a habitat for colonization.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the lack of direct benefit to the bacteria and the substrate specificity of Cgr2

claim: Similar to intestinal and hepatic enzymes, gut bacteria have co-evolved with the human host and maintain detoxification systems that can be rapidly and efficiently mobilized on demand.
source: Although we cannot rule out an as-of-yet unidentified endogenous substrate of Cgr2, our results suggest that similar to intestinal and hepatic enzymes, gut bacteria have co-evolved with the human host and maintain detoxification systems that can be rapidly and efficiently mobilized on demand.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed properties of Cgr2 and analogy to host detoxification systems

claim: Not only do E. lenta strains vary in the presence or absence of cgr2, but a naturally occurring, single amino acid substitution causes a dramatic loss of activity in the Cgr2 enzyme.
source: Our results also highlight an important consideration for ongoing efforts to predict and manipulate gut microbial metabolism, particularly in the context of therapeutics. Not only do E. lenta strains vary in the presence or absence of cgr2, but we have also identified a naturally occurring, single amino acid substitution that causes a dramatic loss of activity in the Cgr2 enzyme.
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and activity assays of the N333 variant

claim: Methods that can achieve nucleotide-level precision in mapping inter-individual differences in human gut microbiome gene content are needed.
source: This result emphasizes the need for methods that can achieve nucleotide-level precision in mapping inter-individual differences in human gut microbiome gene content.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the discovery of functionally significant single nucleotide variants

claim: Several clinical trials have recently investigated the use of digoxin for treating diverse cancers, rheumatoid arthritis and HIV-1 infection.
source: Several clinical trials have recently investigated the use of digoxin for treating diverse cancers (Lin et al., 2014; Kayali et al., 2011), rheumatoid arthritis (Huh et al., 2011) and HIV-1 infection (Wong et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to clinical trial reports

claim: Paired studies of host genetics combined with nucleotide-resolution analyses of the gut microbiome are needed to test the feasibility of using microbial genetic information to predict drug bioavailability and improve treatment outcomes.
source: Paired studies of host genetics combined with nucleotide-resolution analyses of the gut microbiome are needed to test the feasibility of using microbial genetic information to predict drug bioavailability and improve treatment outcomes in these new disease contexts.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future research

claim: The results demonstrate the feasibility of progressing from case studies of a clinically relevant gut microbial biotransformation to identifying the responsible genes, enzymes, and biochemical mechanisms associated with metabolism.
source: Finally, our results demonstrate the feasibility of progressing from case studies of a clinically relevant gut microbial biotransformation (Saha et al., 1983) to identifying the responsible genes, enzymes, and biochemical mechanisms associated with metabolism.
evidence: This is a conclusion about the methodological approach used in the study

claim: The gut microbiome encodes over 3 million genes and >50% have unknown functions.
source: The gut microbiome encodes over 3 million genes (Qin et al., 2010) and >50% have unknown functions (Human Microbiome Project Consortium, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work

claim: Reductive transformations represent a major route by which gut microbes metabolize xenobiotics.
source: As reductive transformations represent a major route by which gut microbes metabolize xenobiotics
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge

claim: Unique, putative reductase enzymes identified in the sequence similarity network provide a promising starting point for identifying additional gut microbiome-xenobiotic interactions.
source: these unique, putative reductase enzymes provide a promising starting point for identifying additional gut microbiome-xenobiotic interactions.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the findings from the sequence similarity network analysis
